Am I required to buy it?

Federal law requires it only in a high-risk zone (A or V) with a federally regulated or backed mortgage, or federal help to buy or build (42 U.S.C. §4012a). Outside those zones, a lender may still require it.

76.4% of Nassau County's NFIP policy units are in high-risk zones (not 76.4% of all buildings, and not an answer about your own home).

Of the NFIP claim dollars paid here (1978–2026), 26.7% went to claims rated outside high-risk zones A and V. That uses the zone on each claim, not today's map, and leaves out claims with no zone.

Flood zonePolicy unitsShare
Zone AE (high-risk)30,07573.4%
Zone X9,51723.2%
Zone VE (high-risk)1,1072.7%
Other high-risk zones (AO, A04, A05, A and others)1340.3%
Other low-risk or unclassified zones1480.4%

Policy records keep the code they were rated with, so older labels such as A1 to A30 are counted on their own. Every zone starting with A or V is high-risk; A1 to A30 and AE are the same kind of area (44 CFR §64.3).

Insured units by the zone each policy is rated in. How this is counted What each means: zone AE, zone X, zone VE.

Flood map: FEMA's latest Community Status Book lists no new flood map taking effect for the towns and areas FEMA lists in this county; that does not cover maps still preliminary (below). FEMA's digital flood map for Nassau County has 140 map panels, the oldest in effect since September 11, 2009 and the newest since September 11, 2009. FEMA has revised that map by 5 Letters of Map Revision, 1 of them in effect since January 1, 2021. FEMA's map service lists 1,237 rulings for owners here who asked FEMA to take a building or lot out of the high-risk zone (Letters of Map Amendment): 774 took the building or some or all of the lot out, 152 found it already outside the zone as mapped, 255 were denied, 56 other or mixed. FEMA charges no review or processing fee for a Letter of Map Amendment request (44 CFR §72.5). FEMA's Online LOMC site lets home owners or their representatives ask FEMA for a Letter of Map Change. Your home may already have an Elevation Certificate on file with your community: ask your local floodplain manager, often in the city or county building, permitting or engineering department. If none is on file, a land surveyor, engineer or architect completes one. These are rulings for owners who chose to apply, so they are not the odds for your home, and FEMA's map service gives no dates for them. They are counted by the towns and areas FEMA lists in this county, so a city that reaches into a neighboring county counts in full here. FEMA's preliminary flood map data give an early look at a home's or community's projected flood risk and may include new or revised flood maps. Check your own address on FEMA's flood map or with our flood zone map lookup by address.

Flood insurance cost in Nassau County, New York

In Nassau County, typically about $1,475 a year ($123 a month), fees included. Half of homeowners here pay between $1,081 and $2,030. To check a quote, use the checker at the top.

A quarter pay under $1,081 · Typical $1,475 · A quarter pay over $2,030 · A tenth pay $3,063 or more

Each policy's annual cost (premium plus the federal policy fee, reserve fund assessment and HFIAA surcharge), single-family primary residences. The bar is the middle half of policies, from 29,979 single-family primary-home policies. These are existing policies, many still below FEMA's full-risk price.

The NFIP also offers policies for renters and businesses. The median here is for single-family primary-home policies, not businesses or second homes. Renting? See what renters pay.

Source: floodsmart.gov (official pages, checked October 25, 2026). Not endorsed by FEMA.

How do I actually get covered — and how fast?

Most policies start 30 days after you buy. Bought while making, increasing, extending or renewing a mortgage, it can start at closing if the insurer is paid within 10 days (30 if the lender, title company or settlement attorney pays).

  • Waiting period30 days
  • Bought with a new or refinanced mortgageCan start at closing, if paid in time
  • NFIP building limit$250,000
  • NFIP contents limit$100,000

Most homeowners insurance does not cover flood damage. To buy: call the NFIP at (877) 336-2627, go to FloodSmart.gov, or ask any licensed insurance agent. Every NFIP insurer offers the same rates.

Already flooded? Insured: report the loss to your insurance agent or company now (FEMA's steps: how to start a flood claim), and send a proof of loss (your signed, sworn statement of the amount you are claiming) within 60 days of the flood (44 CFR 61, App. A(1), Art. VII). Not insured: a policy bought today will not cover a flood that already happened, and FEMA disaster aid is open to people in counties designated in a federally declared disaster.

Exceptions to the thirty-day wait, what a policy won't pay (wind, outside belongings, living costs), premium increases, FEMA aid vs insurance, appeals, the substantial-damage rebuilding rule and the rules at a closing: the NFIP rules in full, each with its official source.

Your state's insurance regulator: New York Department of Financial Services.

Source: floodsmart.gov, agents.floodsmart.gov, fema.gov, ecfr.gov (official pages, checked October 25, 2026). Not endorsed by FEMA.

Flood insurance claims in Nassau County, New York: what floods pay out

Floods in Nassau County have led to 50,471 NFIP flood claims and $2.3 billion in payouts since 1978; the worst years were 2012, 2011 and 1992.

Bar height is dollars paid that year. Orange bars are the three costliest years: 2012 ($1,987,000,514), 2011 ($133,614,690), 1992 ($37,743,652). Total paid $2,258,579,240. Totals for 2025 and 2026 are not final while their claims stay open. How this is counted

Outside the high-risk zones: of the 1,959 claims here with a flood zone on the claim, losses 2016–2025, 24.0% were rated outside zones A and V (zones X, B, C and D), and they got 28.5% of the dollars paid on those claims. The zone is the one on each claim, not today's map; claims with no zone on them are left out.

Do flood claims here actually pay out?

Most do: 88.2% of claims in Nassau County paid something. The average paid claim was $51,134 (all years, in dollars of the day, not adjusted for inflation).

Typical claim: the median paid building claim was $25,127; Hurricane Sandy alone paid $2.0 billion including code-upgrade (ICC) pay, which pulls the average up.

FEMA's claim records give a reason when a building claim has no recorded payment, such as damage less than the deductible, not an actual flood, seepage or backed-up drains. The average is over claims that paid something and includes Increased Cost of Compliance payments (help to elevate or rebuild to code), which the yearly totals above leave out. Dollars are as paid at the time, not adjusted for inflation; a single home can file across several floods over the years. These shares count every FEMA claim record from every year except records FEMA coded "deleted in error" or "assigned in error"; the claims page counts only losses from 2020 on, so its shares differ. FEMA's data has no open or closed field, so a recent claim with no payment may still be paid.

Would a policy here pay to rebuild my home?

Not in full for at least 60.0% of the 23,262 single-family policies here that report a rebuilding cost: FEMA's records put it above the NFIP's $250,000 building limit.

  • Rebuilding cost above the building limit (of 23,262 policies reporting one)60.0%New York: 53.6%
  • Single-family policies insured to the building maximum (all of them, not only those above)91.6%
  • Damage was more than the coverage (of 43,477 claims paid with a damage figure)2.0%

The two shares have different bases: insured-to-the-maximum counts every single-family policy with the full building limit; the rebuilding-cost share counts only the policies that report a rebuilding cost. Homes insured for less than their own rebuilding cost can also fall short. How this is counted

The NFIP pays the cost to rebuild (not a depreciated value) only for a single-family home that is your principal residence and is insured for at least 80% of its full rebuilding cost, or for the $250,000 maximum.

Source: FEMA OpenFEMA — NFIP Policies; FEMA OpenFEMA — NFIP Claims. Data effective August 31, 2026; retrieved November 11, 2026.

What does it cost in my flood zone?

From about $1,147 a year (Zone X) to $2,411 (Zone AO) here. Your zone is on your lender's flood determination or FEMA's map; find its row below.

What the zone codes mean (44 CFR §64.3): A, AE and A1–A30 are high-risk; AO and AH are high-risk with shallow flooding; A99 is high-risk behind a flood barrier FEMA treats as complete; V, VE and V1–V30 are coastal high-risk, flooded by tides with fast-moving water (velocity); B and X are areas of moderate flood hazard, C and X areas of minimal hazard; D has possible but undetermined flood hazards. A 1 percent or greater chance a year works out to a 26% or greater chance of at least one such flood over 30 years.

Zones with fewer than 50 priced single-family policies are omitted. Your own premium still depends on elevation and coverage.

How much flood risk is here?

Very High for coastal flooding and Relatively High for inland (river) flooding, by FEMA's county rating. That compares this county with others; it is not a forecast for your address.

  • Coastal flood risk rating (FEMA)Very High
  • Inland flood risk rating (FEMA)Relatively High

FEMA's rating weighs modeled loss with social vulnerability and community resilience; it is not a prediction for your home, and it can differ from the loss percentile below. Coastal: FEMA models roughly $24.3 million of flood loss a year (buildings, people and farmland valued in dollars, insured or not; a model, not insurance payouts); a separate FEMA measure, loss per dollar of building value: coastal flood loss here is higher than in about 86% of U.S. counties. Inland: FEMA models roughly $183.9 million of flood loss a year (buildings, people and farmland valued in dollars, insured or not; a model, not insurance payouts); a separate FEMA measure, loss per dollar of building value: inland flood loss here is higher than in about 18% of U.S. counties. Loss figures model all flood loss, insured or not, so they run far above insurance payouts. How this is counted

Source: FEMA — National Risk Index (flood). Data: NRI December 2025 release; retrieved November 11, 2026.

Local sea level: NOAA's tide gauge at Kings Point measured a sea-level trend of +1.08 inches per decade (give or take 0.04 inches per decade) from 1931 to 2025. A plus sign means the water there got higher over that period. A tide gauge measures one spot on the coast; it is not your property's flood risk.

Source: NOAA Tides & Currents — Sea Level Trends. Data: NOAA's published trends; retrieved November 11, 2026.

How often is this county a flood disaster?

17 federal disasters for floods or storms here; the latest was Severe Storm and Flooding (2024).

  • September 2021 — Remnants of Hurricane Ida
  • September 2021 — Remnants of Hurricane Ida (emergency declaration)

Only the latest are listed, newest first; disasters with the same month and title share one line, which says how many; the count covers every flood, hurricane, tropical-storm and coastal-storm declaration FEMA lists here, plus severe-storm declarations whose title names flooding, including emergency declarations. How this is counted

Source: FEMA OpenFEMA — Disaster Declarations Summaries. Data: declarations through 2024; retrieved November 11, 2026.

Did FEMA aid homeowners after floods and storms?

Yes: FEMA approved $285.1 million for homeowners here after floods and storms, about $4,609 per registration.

FEMA disaster aid helps with uninsured and underinsured losses, and is separate from NFIP insurance. The average is over every registration, including those approved for nothing. Only disasters counted in the flood-disaster card are included; their aid can still cover wind or tornado damage from the same storm. Disasters for COVID, fire, winter storms or tornadoes alone are left out.

Source: FEMA OpenFEMA — Housing Assistance (Owners). Data: homeowner aid by disaster; retrieved November 11, 2026.
